To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) dieting in the healthy normal weight range is a strong predictor of subsequent weight gain; (b) fat overshooting is the central outcome of body weight regulation; and (c) fat overshooting may be a consequence of the preferential catch‐ up fat that is a central component of body composition autostabilization in the healthy normal‐weight range.

repeated dieting to regain body fat mass (i) is a prerequisite for full recovery of FFM, (ii) is accompanied by excess fat deposition, (iii) results in a state hyperphagia beyond full recovery of fat mass, and (iv) is accompanied by a preferential catch‐ up fat relative to FFM.

repeated dieting in normal weight people is a risk factor for fatness because it results in fat overshooting, which is a consequence of preferential catch‐ up fat, and this in turn is due to a desynchronization in the rate of recovery of fat mass vs. fat‐free mass.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the body regulates its energy stores (body composition) in response to dieting and how the body composition autoregoles in response to diet and refeeding.

the biological and metabolic consequences of dieting and weight loss, with the ultimate goal to understand the biological mechanisms underlying the relationship between dieting and weight gain and to develop effective and sustainable strategies to prevent obesity and its associated metabolic disorders.
the mechanisms by which dieting and weight loss in the normal‐weight population predispose to weight regain, and how these mechanisms may be related to obesity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is strong that dieting makes the healthy normal fatter, whereas the evidence is inconclusive that it makes the overweight and obese fatter.
dieting in the normal‐weight does not cause weight gain, but rather that it is the weight gain itself that may be a consequence of dieting.
repeated dieting to maintain or lose body weight in normal‐ or under‐weight people, and in the absence of a clear genetic predisposition to obesity, is a risk factor for future fatness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dieting to lose body fat in normal‐weight individuals, rather than in overweight and obese people, may be a contributing factor to weight regain and the development of obesity.
the biological plausibilities that underlie the adverse health consequences of dieting are the same that underlie the obesity epidemic.
repeated dieting to achieve weight loss and/or optimize performance in lean people may be a contributing factor to weight gain and the obesity epidemic.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the body composition autoregregulatory process of fat overshooting, which is triggered by repeated energy restriction, is a plausible biological mechanism to explain why dieting makes the healthy lean fatter.

the risks for weight regain and weight cycling may not only be due to the loss of energy stores and metabolic adaptations to weight loss, but also due to the loss and recovery of body composition, i.e. body composition autoregluation.

the biological plausibilities that repeated dieting and subsequent weight cycling may contribute to the obesity epidemic are supported by the results of experimental studies of human body composition.
